question: What is a JWT and what is it made of?
title: JWT Structure Explained – Java Backend Security Interview
direct_answer: A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a compact format for carrying claims between parties. The common signed form is a JWS with three Base64URL segments: protected header, payload, and signature. The header identifies the signing algorithm and often a key ID; the payload contains claims such as `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, and `exp`; the signature lets a verifier detect changes and authenticate the issuer's key. Base64URL is encoding, not encryption. An encrypted JWT uses JWE and has a different five-part compact form.

sections.title: JWT: Claims in a Signed or Encrypted Token
sections.content:
A **JWT (JSON Web Token)** is a standard way to carry a set of JSON claims. In the common signed form, the JWT is a compact **JWS** with three Base64URL segments separated by dots.

The protected header says how the token was signed and may include a key identifier. The payload contains claims: `iss` identifies the issuer, `sub` identifies the subject, `aud` names the intended recipient, and `exp` limits the token's lifetime. The signature covers the encoded header and payload. A verifier must use a trusted key, allow the expected algorithm, and validate relevant claims before using the data.

Anyone holding an ordinary signed JWT can decode its header and payload. The signature provides integrity and issuer authentication, not secrecy. Sensitive content needs a different design; JWT can also use encrypted JWE, whose compact form has five parts.

sections.title: The Three Parts of a JWT at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|Protected header|~first JWS segment|algorithm and optional key ID|Base64URL-encoded|input to signature
emerald|Payload|~second JWS segment|registered and custom claims|Base64URL-encoded|readable unless encrypted
rose|Signature|~third JWS segment|covers header + payload|verified with trusted key|detects modification
amber|JWE variant|~encrypted JWT|five compact segments|provides confidentiality|different from three-part signed JWS

sections.title: Creating and Validating a JWT in Spring Boot
When to Use JWT
sections.content:
Use JWTs when you need **stateless authentication** across multiple servers or microservices — for example, a Spring Boot API deployed on three EC2 instances behind a load balancer, where any instance should authenticate a user without calling a shared session database.

Use them for **mobile app backends** where session cookies don't work well and you want the app to send the token in the Authorization header.

Use them in **single sign-on (SSO)** scenarios where a user logs in once and the token grants access to multiple services.

Avoid JWTs if you need frequent token revocation (like admin-triggered logout) — the stateless nature makes immediate revocation difficult unless you maintain a blacklist, which defeats the statelessness benefit.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating the payload as encrypted**: Freshers often think JWT hides the data because it looks encoded. The payload is only Base64URL-encoded — anyone can decode it and read the claims. Never put passwords, credit card numbers, or API keys in a JWT payload.
- **Not validating the signature**: Some implementations extract the payload without calling parseClaimsJws(), which skips signature verification. An attacker can then modify the token and the server will trust it. Always validate before using claims.
- **Using weak or hardcoded secrets**: Using "secret" or "12345" as the signing key makes JWTs trivially forgeable. In production, use a strong random key stored in environment variables, rotated regularly.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- A JWT carries JSON claims; the common signed form is a three-part compact JWS.
- Header and payload are Base64URL-encoded, not hidden.
- The signature protects integrity only when verified with a trusted key and expected algorithm.
- Validate issuer, audience, expiry, not-before, and any application-specific claims you rely on.
- An encrypted JWT uses JWE and has five compact segments.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A JWT is a standard token format for carrying JSON claims. The form most APIs use is a signed JWS with three Base64URL segments separated by dots. The protected header identifies the signing algorithm and may contain a key ID. The payload contains claims such as issuer, subject, audience, and expiry. The signature covers the encoded header and payload, so a verifier with the trusted key can detect any change.

Base64URL is only an encoding. Anyone who receives an ordinary signed JWT can read its header and payload, so passwords, private keys, and other secrets do not belong there. The signature supplies integrity and helps authenticate the issuer's key; it does not encrypt the claims.

Verification must include more than checking that a signature exists. The service should allow only its expected algorithms and keys, then validate issuer, audience, expiry, not-before, and any claims used for authorization. JWT can also be encrypted as JWE, whose compact form has five segments, so “three parts” specifically describes the common signed form.

question: How does JWT-based authentication work in a Spring Boot REST API?
title: JWT Authentication Flow in Spring Boot REST API
direct_answer: In a Spring Boot API, an authorization service first authenticates the user and issues a signed access token. On later requests, Spring Security's OAuth2 Resource Server support reads the bearer token, verifies it with a configured `JwtDecoder`, validates claims such as issuer and expiry, converts accepted claims to authorities, and places the resulting `Authentication` in the `SecurityContext`. Request or method authorization then decides access. A custom `OncePerRequestFilter` is possible, but it is not the normal starting point.

sections.title: JWT Authentication Flow in Spring Boot REST API
sections.content:
JWT authentication has two roles. An **authorization server** or login service checks the user's credentials and issues a signed access token. The protected Spring Boot API acts as a **resource server** and validates that token on every request.

Spring Security reads `Authorization: Bearer ...`, passes the value to a configured `JwtDecoder`, verifies the signature, and validates claims such as issuer, expiry, and not-before. The decoder or added validators should also enforce the intended audience when the token is audience-bound. Accepted scopes or roles are converted to `GrantedAuthority` values, and Spring places an authenticated object in the `SecurityContext` for the request.

Authorization runs after authentication. A missing or invalid bearer token commonly leads to 401; a valid principal without the required authority commonly leads to 403. `SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS` prevents Spring Security from using an HTTP session to persist the context between requests.

sections.title: Request Flow Through the JWT Filter
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Authorization service verifies login] --> B[Issue signed access token]
    B --> C[Client sends Authorization: Bearer token]
    C --> D[BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter]
    D --> E[JwtDecoder verifies signature and claims]
    E -->|Invalid| F[401 response]
    E -->|Valid| G[Convert claims to authorities]
    G --> H[Authentication in SecurityContext]
    H --> I{Authorized for endpoint?}
    I -->|No| J[403 response]
    I -->|Yes| K[Controller runs]
```

sections.title: JWT Authentication Filter in Spring Security
sections.content:
```java
@Bean
SecurityFilterChain apiSecurity(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    http
        .securityMatcher("/api/**")
        .sessionManagement(sm -> sm.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(resourceServer -> resourceServer.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasAuthority("SCOPE_admin")
            .anyRequest().authenticated());
    return http.build();
}
```
```properties
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri=https://auth.example
```
*With issuer discovery configured, Spring obtains trusted signing keys and validates the token issuer and time claims. Add an audience validator when the issuer serves tokens for more than one resource.*

sections.title: When to Use JWT Authentication
sections.content:
Use JWT-based auth for **RESTful APIs** consumed by mobile apps, SPAs (single-page applications), or third-party services where session cookies aren't practical.

Use it when you need to **scale horizontally** — multiple Spring Boot instances behind a load balancer, where session replication would be complex and slow.

Use it in **microservices architectures** where each service needs to validate user identity without calling a central auth server every time — the JWT carries the necessary claims.

Avoid JWT if your use case requires **frequent token revocation** (like a banking app where you need to instantly invalidate tokens if fraud is detected) — JWTs are hard to revoke because they're stateless. In those cases, consider using opaque tokens with server-side validation or a hybrid approach with a token blacklist.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting to set sessionCreationPolicy to STATELESS**: Freshers often leave the default session policy, so Spring creates HTTP sessions even though you're using JWT. This defeats the purpose and wastes memory. Always configure SecurityConfig with sessionManagement().sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS).
- **Not checking if Authentication is already set**: The filter runs on every request, and if you don't check SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication() == null, you might reprocess the same token multiple times or override existing authentication. The null check prevents redundant work.
- **Validating the token after setting SecurityContext**: Some implementations extract the username, set authentication, then validate — by that point the request is already authenticated with potentially invalid data. Always validate the token signature BEFORE setting the Authentication object.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Token issuance and API validation are separate responsibilities.
- OAuth2 Resource Server reads the bearer token and delegates verification to `JwtDecoder`.
- Validate the trusted key and expected algorithm plus issuer, audience, and time claims.
- Accepted claims become authorities and an `Authentication` in the request `SecurityContext`.
- Authorization follows authentication; a custom JWT filter is not the default requirement.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
JWT authentication in a Spring Boot API has an issuance step and a request-validation step. An authorization service first verifies the login and issues a signed access token. The client then sends that token as `Authorization: Bearer ...` when it calls the API.

Spring Security's OAuth2 Resource Server support extracts the bearer token and gives it to a `JwtDecoder`. The decoder verifies the signature with a trusted key and validates claims such as issuer, expiry, and not-before. The service should also validate audience when the token is meant for a particular API. Spring converts accepted scopes or roles into authorities and creates an `Authentication` in the `SecurityContext` for that request.

Request or method authorization then checks whether those authorities allow the action. A missing or invalid token commonly produces 401, while a valid token without permission commonly produces 403. A stateless policy means the context is rebuilt from the token on each request rather than stored in an HTTP session. Spring already provides this flow; a hand-written `OncePerRequestFilter` is only needed for a genuinely non-standard token scheme.

question: What are the security risks of using JWT and how do you mitigate them?
title: JWT Security Risks and Mitigations – Java Backend
direct_answer: JWT failures usually come from incorrect verification, exposed signing keys, readable sensitive claims, stolen tokens, stale authorization, and weak expiry or refresh design. Use a maintained JOSE library, allow only expected algorithms and key types, obtain keys from a trusted issuer, validate issuer, audience and time claims, keep claims minimal, use TLS, and choose bounded lifetimes from the system's risk. Plan refresh-token rotation, reuse detection, or server-side revocation where immediate invalidation is required.

sections.title: JWT Security Vulnerabilities and Defense Strategies
sections.content:
While JWTs provide a convenient mechanism for stateless authentication, they introduce several security risks that freshers often overlook. The most critical vulnerability is **algorithm confusion**, where an attacker changes the header to alg:none (no signature) and the server accepts it if not properly configured.

Another major issue is **secret key leakage** — if your signing key is exposed (hardcoded in Git, logged, or insufficiently random), attackers can forge valid tokens for any user. JWTs are also **difficult to revoke** because they're stateless — if a token is stolen, it remains valid until expiry. The **payload is readable** by anyone who base64-decodes it, so sensitive data exposure is a risk. **Client-side storage** introduces vulnerabilities: localStorage is accessible to JavaScript (XSS attacks), and cookies without proper flags are vulnerable to CSRF. Finally, **missing expiration** or overly long expiry times mean stolen tokens have a long attack window. Understanding these risks and implementing mitigations is what separates security-aware developers from those who just follow tutorials.

sections.title: JWT Risks Mapped to Mitigations
sections.content:
rose|Verification error|~wrong algorithm/key/issuer|token accepted for wrong trust boundary|use maintained library + allowlist|validate issuer and audience
amber|Key exposure|~forged tokens|hardcoded or leaked signing key|managed secret or key service|rotate with key IDs
violet|Stolen/stale token|~replay or old permissions|bearer token works until rejected|bounded lifetime + revocation design|refresh rotation and reuse detection
cyan|Readable claims|~data disclosure|signed payload is not encrypted|minimize claims|use JWE only when justified

sections.title: Secure JWT Configuration in Spring Boot
When to Apply JWT Security Mitigations
sections.content:
Apply **algorithm enforcement and key rotation** in all production JWT implementations — these are non-negotiable baseline defenses.

Use **short-lived access tokens (15-30 minutes) with refresh tokens** when you need a balance between security and user experience — the user stays logged in, but stolen access tokens expire quickly. Implement a **token blacklist** when handling high-value operations like financial transactions, admin actions, or account deletion, where you need the ability to immediately invalidate a token despite JWT being stateless.

Use **HttpOnly cookies with SameSite** for web applications to prevent XSS token theft.

Apply **payload encryption** (using JWE instead of JWT) only when you must include sensitive data that can't be stored elsewhere — but prefer redesigning to avoid putting sensitive data in tokens at all. In microservices, consider **RS256 (RSA signatures)** instead of HS256 so public keys can be distributed without exposing signing ability.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Not validating the algorithm in the header**: Freshers call parseClaimsJws() but don't realize some libraries accept alg:none if not explicitly blocked. Always use parserBuilder().setSigningKey() which enforces signature validation — never parse the token manually with string splitting.
- **Storing the secret key in application.properties committed to Git**: The signing key should be an environment variable or secret manager entry, never hardcoded or version-controlled. Use at minimum a 256-bit random key for HS256.
- **Setting expiration to days or weeks**: A 7-day token gives attackers a week-long attack window if stolen. Use 15-30 minute access tokens with a separate refresh token for longer sessions.
- **Implementing blacklist in application memory**: Using a simple HashSet means the blacklist is lost on server restart and isn't shared across instances. Use Redis or a database for distributed blacklist storage.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- Use a maintained JOSE library and allow only the algorithms and key types expected by the service.
- Validate signature, issuer, audience, expiry, not-before, and application claims before use.
- Signed JWT claims are readable; keep sensitive and rapidly changing data out.
- A stolen bearer token can be replayed until it expires or a revocation check rejects it.
- Choose lifetimes and refresh/revocation controls from risk; there is no universal number.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A JWT is safe only when the whole verification and lifecycle design is safe. The API must use a maintained JOSE library, restrict verification to the expected algorithms and key types, obtain keys from a trusted issuer, and validate issuer, audience, expiry, not-before, and any claims used for authorization. Simply decoding the payload is not authentication.

For example, an Orders API should reject a correctly signed token whose `aud` names the Billing API, and it should not accept an attacker-selected `alg` just because the token header requests it. A signed JWT is readable, so it should carry only the claims the API needs; passwords and other secrets do not belong in it.

A stolen access token can be replayed until it expires or a server-side check rejects it. Bounded access-token lifetime reduces that window, while refresh-token rotation with reuse detection can limit refresh replay. Systems that need immediate logout or permission changes need a revocation, token-version, or introspection design. Those controls add state deliberately; JWT does not remove the need to manage security state.

question: Where should you store a JWT on the client side?
title: Where to Store JWT on Client Side – Security Tradeoffs
direct_answer: There is no universally safest browser location for a JWT. Avoid long-lived bearer tokens in `localStorage` or `sessionStorage` because injected JavaScript can read and export them. An access token kept only in memory has less persistence but active malicious script can still use it. A Secure, HttpOnly cookie prevents JavaScript from reading the credential, but the browser sends it automatically, so the server must use CSRF defenses and a suitable SameSite policy. For many browser apps, a backend-for-frontend that keeps OAuth tokens server-side and exposes only a hardened session cookie gives the browser the least token access.

sections.title: Client-Side JWT Storage: Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
Where you store a JWT on the client determines its attack surface.

The main threat models are **XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)**, where malicious JavaScript steals the token, and **CSRF (Cross-Site Request Forgery)**, where an attacker tricks the browser into making authenticated requests. **LocalStorage** and **sessionStorage** are vulnerable to XSS — any JavaScript on the page can read them, including injected malicious scripts. **Memory storage** (just a JavaScript variable) is XSS-resistant because it's not accessible across page reloads, but it's lost when the user refreshes. **HttpOnly cookies** are the most secure because the browser automatically includes them in requests, but JavaScript cannot access them, blocking XSS attacks. However, cookies introduce **CSRF risk** — a malicious site can trigger requests to your API with the cookie attached. The mitigation is the **SameSite** attribute (Strict or Lax), which tells the browser to only send the cookie for same-site requests. The best practice is **HttpOnly cookie with SameSite=Strict** — it prevents both XSS and CSRF at the cost of slightly more complex backend configuration.

rows: High: injected script can read and export bearer tokens
Active script can still use it; less persistent after reload
Often paired with a careful renewal flow
Script cannot read the cookie value
Needs CSRF protection and suitable SameSite policy
OAuth tokens stay on the server
Cookie session still needs CSRF protection
Reduces token exposure in browser code

sections.title: Insecure: Returning the Token for localStorage
Cookie Session: Protect Reading and Forged Requests
sections.content:
```java
ResponseCookie session = ResponseCookie.from("SESSION", opaqueSessionId)
    .httpOnly(true)
    .secure(true)
    .sameSite("Lax")
    .path("/")
    .build();

return ResponseEntity.noContent()
    .header(HttpHeaders.SET_COOKIE, session.toString())
    .build();
```
*HttpOnly prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie value. Because the browser sends the cookie automatically, keep Spring CSRF protection enabled for unsafe requests. Choose Lax, Strict, or None from the actual cross-site flow rather than using one value universally.*

sections.title: Storage Options at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|Web Storage|~bearer token readable by script|easy persistence|one XSS can export token|avoid for long-lived sessions
amber|Memory|~less persistent|lost on reload|active XSS can still call APIs|renewal design needed
blue|HttpOnly cookie|~not readable by JS|automatically sent|requires CSRF defense|SameSite depends on flow
emerald|Backend for frontend|~tokens held server-side|browser gets session cookie|smaller browser token surface|more server responsibility

sections.title: When to Use Each Storage Option
sections.content:
Use **HttpOnly cookie with SameSite=Strict** for production web applications where security is critical — this is the recommended default for SPAs and server-rendered apps.

Use **memory storage** during development or for high-security apps where you're okay with the user logging in again on every page refresh — some banking apps do this intentionally.

Use **sessionStorage** (with caution) if you need the token to survive refresh but want it cleared when the user closes the browser tab — still vulnerable to XSS, so only for lower-risk apps. **Avoid localStorage** in production unless you've done a thorough XSS risk assessment — it's the most dangerous option despite being the simplest. For mobile apps or Electron desktop apps, the threat model is different (no XSS/CSRF), so secure platform storage like iOS Keychain or Android Keystore is preferred. Never use localStorage if your app has any user-generated content or third-party scripts.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Choosing localStorage for convenience**: Freshers often pick localStorage because tutorials show it and it's just two lines of code (localStorage.setItem, localStorage.getItem). Interviewers see this as a security red flag. Any XSS vulnerability — even from a third-party script or a comment section — can steal the token. Always articulate why you'd avoid it.
- **Not setting SameSite on cookies**: Setting a cookie without SameSite leaves it vulnerable to CSRF attacks where a malicious site triggers authenticated requests. Always specify SameSite=Strict or Lax. Strict is more secure (cookie only sent for same-site navigation), Lax allows some cross-site scenarios like following a link.
- **Assuming HttpOnly means the cookie can't be sent in requests**: HttpOnly means JavaScript can't read the cookie value, but the browser still automatically includes it in HTTP requests to the same domain — that's the whole point. This isn't a vulnerability, it's the intended behavior.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- There is no single best storage choice for every client and architecture.
- Avoid long-lived bearer tokens in web storage because JavaScript can export them after XSS.
- Memory reduces persistence, but active injected script can still act as the user.
- HttpOnly blocks reading a cookie value; it does not stop authenticated actions and it introduces CSRF concerns.
- A backend-for-frontend can keep OAuth access and refresh tokens out of browser code.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
There is no universally best place to store a JWT in a browser because each choice moves risk. A bearer token in `localStorage` or `sessionStorage` is easy for client code to use, but injected JavaScript can read and export it. Keeping an access token only in memory reduces persistence across reloads, although active malicious script can still call the API while the page is open.

A Secure, HttpOnly cookie prevents JavaScript from reading the credential value. That helps against token exfiltration, but the browser sends the cookie automatically, so unsafe requests need CSRF protection and an appropriate SameSite policy. HttpOnly also does not stop injected script from performing actions through the trusted page.

For many browser applications, a backend-for-frontend is a strong design: OAuth tokens remain on the server and the browser receives only a hardened session cookie. That cookie still needs CSRF protection. The final choice depends on whether the client is a browser or native app, the origin layout, persistence needs, XSS exposure, and how renewal and logout must work.

question: How do you handle JWT expiry and token refresh?
title: JWT Expiry and Token Refresh – Java Backend Interview
direct_answer: The resource server rejects an access token after its `exp` time. A client may then use a separately protected refresh token at the authorization server to obtain a new access token, but it should not refresh blindly for every 401. Access and refresh lifetimes are chosen from risk and user experience rather than fixed numbers. For higher-risk clients, rotate refresh tokens, store each active token or family server-side, and detect reuse so a replay can revoke the affected family.

sections.title: JWT Lifecycle Management with Access and Refresh Tokens
sections.content:
An access token has an expiration time and is presented to a resource server. Once `exp` has passed, the resource server rejects it. The client can ask the **authorization server** for another access token only if it has a valid refresh token or it reauthenticates.

Refresh tokens are longer-lived credentials, not API tokens. They may be opaque rather than JWTs and should be stored more carefully than access tokens. Their lifetime depends on the client type, data sensitivity, compromise detection, and acceptable sign-in frequency; no fixed “15 minutes and 7 days” rule fits every system.

With refresh-token rotation, each successful use produces a replacement and invalidates the old token in one atomic operation. If an invalidated token appears again, the server treats it as possible replay and can revoke the whole token family. Rotation without reuse detection and transactional updates does not fully address theft.

sections.title: Access + Refresh Token Lifecycle
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Authorization server issues access + refresh credentials] --> B[Client calls resource server with access token]
    B --> C{Access token accepted?}
    C -->|Yes| B
    C -->|Expired| D[Client may call token endpoint with refresh token]
    D --> E{Refresh token valid and current?}
    E -->|No or reused| F[Revoke family and require sign-in]
    E -->|Yes| G[Atomically rotate refresh token and issue access token]
    G --> B
```

sections.title: Spring Boot Token Refresh Flow with Rotation
When to Use This Dual-Token Pattern
sections.content:
Use this pattern in **production REST APIs** where users stay logged in for extended periods (web apps, mobile apps). If your app is a single-page application (SPA) where users work for hours, you can't keep popping login screens every 15 minutes. The refresh mechanism keeps sessions alive without storing passwords.

Use **refresh token rotation** in high-security contexts like banking or healthcare apps — each refresh burns the old token, so even if an attacker intercepts one, it's a one-time-use window. Skip this complexity for **internal tools** with 8-hour sessions or **short-lived dashboards** where users don't mind re-authenticating. For **server-to-server APIs** (microservices calling each other), client credentials flow with long-lived access tokens is simpler since there's no user session to maintain.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Setting 7-day expiry on access tokens**: Freshers avoid refresh logic by making access tokens live for days. This defeats the purpose — a stolen token is valid for a week. Access tokens should be short (15-60 min) so compromised tokens expire quickly.
- **Storing refresh tokens in localStorage**: Browser localStorage is vulnerable to XSS attacks. Store refresh tokens in httpOnly secure cookies or in-memory variables for SPAs. If using cookies, set SameSite=Strict to prevent CSRF.
- **Not invalidating refresh tokens on logout**: Freshers forget to delete refresh tokens from the database on logout. If a user logs out, their refresh token should be immediately revoked so no one can use it to mint new access tokens.
- **Allowing unlimited refresh token reuse**: Without rotation, a leaked refresh token can be used indefinitely until it expires. Each refresh should invalidate the old token and issue a new one.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- The resource server rejects an access token after `exp`; the authorization server handles refresh.
- Refresh tokens are separate high-value credentials and need stronger storage and audience limits.
- Lifetimes are risk-based, not universal constants.
- Rotation must invalidate the old token atomically; reuse detection can revoke the token family.
- Do not refresh blindly on every 401, because 401 can have causes other than expiry.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
An access token is accepted only until its expiry time. After that, the resource server rejects it. A client can obtain another access token from the authorization server by presenting a separate refresh token, or the user can authenticate again. The refresh token is not sent to normal APIs and may be an opaque random value rather than a JWT.

The access-token and refresh-token lifetimes depend on risk, client type, data sensitivity, and acceptable sign-in frequency. Shorter access-token life reduces the replay window, while a longer refresh credential improves usability but needs stronger storage and control. There is no universal 15-minute or seven-day setting.

For clients that use refresh-token rotation, the server invalidates the presented token and creates a replacement in one atomic operation. If an old token is later reused, that can signal theft, and the server can revoke the token family and require sign-in. The client should refresh only when it knows expiry is the cause, not retry every 401 forever.
